power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: In experiment 2, changing the prompting protocol altered MedQA accuracy by -11•3 to +9•3 percentage points relative to the default prompt (figure 4B; appendix p 14-15). The direction and magnitude of these changes depended on the model. A chain-of-thought cue increased accuracy for Llama 3.1 8B by 9•3 percentage points (95% CI 1•0-17•5), but decreased accuracy for Qwen2.5 7B by 11•3 percentage points (4•0-18•4). However, none of the 12 protocol comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm correction; the smallest adjusted p value was 0•055. Approximately 19% of questions changed from correct to incorrect, or vice versa, between protocols. Based on this observed discordance, approximately 600 questions would be required to detect a 5-percentage-point protocol effect with 80% power. In experiment 3, repeated runs at temperature 0 produced identical results for both models. At temperature 0•7, however, run-to-run variability differed between models. Llama 3.1 8B achieved accuracies ranging from 51•3% to 59•3% across the three runs (SD 4•1 percentage points), with identical outcomes across all three runs for only 59•3% of questions. Gemma 3 27B was substantially more stable, with accuracy ranging from 74•7% to 75•3% and identical outcomes across all three runs for 98•7% of questions (figure 4C; appendix p 15).

text.text: Background Large language models (LLMs) are solely judged by their scores on biomedical benchmarks, yet these scores are rarely reproducible since the prompts, inference settings and model builds are seldom reported.
We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source platform for auditable evaluation of language and vision-language models for biomedical research.
Methods BenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub.
text.formatted: Methods BenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub">https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub</ref>.

text.text: The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records.
The platform samples questions with fixed seeds, runs models directly or as toolusing agents in a code sandbox, grades answers with deterministic rules and stores every prompt, reply and tool call.
The interface provides a leaderboard to rank performance of the models, allowing model comparison without any preexisting programming knowledge.
Findings We used BenchmarkHub to evaluate 12 open-weight models in five experiments on 15 biomedical benchmarks (11 text, two multimodal and two computational biology) and two general benchmarks.
The pooled accuracy ranged from 46•1% (95% CI 43•0-49•3) to 80•9% (78•3-83•3).
Re-grading the responses with simple answer-extraction rules lowered a model's accuracy by up to 33•1 percentage points leading to a reorder of the leaderboard.
Published scores were found for 23 out of the 143 benchmark/model combinations tested.
The accuracy measured by BenchmarkHub was lower than in the published results in 19 out of the 23.

from preprints or developer-run evaluations, and we found no medical study that quantified, on the same items and within one framework, the effects of prompting protocol, answer extraction, image availability and tool access, nor an open, self-hosted platform built for that purpose.

BenchmarkHub is, to our knowledge, the first open-source platform that combines a web interface, command-line and REST access, local and cloud model providers, a sandboxed tool-use agent loop, procedurally generated computational biology benchmarks and a complete per-question audit trail.

Using only the platform and 12 locally served open-weight models, we show that the answer-extraction rule alone can change medical accuracy by more than the gaps between models and reorder them, that published scores are usually higher than those measured under a documented protocol, that protocol effects need larger samples than are typically used, that on a medical multimodal benchmark the strongest models kept about 90% of their accuracy without the images, and that tool access transforms performance on computational biology tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) currently need to pass medical licensing-style examinations. 1 Multiple-choice benchmarks such as MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and the medical subsets of MMLU have become the default evidence offered for their medical competence. [2] [3] [4] [5] A systematic review of 519 evaluation studies found that most assessed accuracy is on examstyle questions and only 5% used real patient data. 6 Benchmark accuracy also transfers poorly to real-world use: although LLMs identified at least one relevant medical condition in 94•9% of scenarios when assessed independently, members of the public using the same models . identified relevant conditions in fewer than 34•5% of cases, performing no better than participants who used other sources of information.

text.text: We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source, self-hostable platform that makes every step of the evaluation pipeline an explicit, recorded and re-runnable variable, and that extends evaluation from single-turn questions to tool-using agents.

Here we describe the platform and report five use cases, run entirely through its public API on locally served open-weight models, that quantify how answer extraction, prompting protocol, image availability and tool access change medical and biomedical results.
BenchmarkHub is available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub.

text.text: BenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence.

The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Models are reached through provider adapters for local inference servers (Ollama, vLLM and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) and for cloud APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Groq and Cohere).
When a local server is used, prompts, questions and outputs never leave the institution.
Per-provider concurrency limits and retry policies protect shared inference servers.
The platform ships loaders for 65 benchmarks, including 16 medical, clinical or biomedical datasets and ten additional ones for bioinformatics questions.
Users can add their own questions from CSV files, the Hugging Face Hub or document collections.

A run is defined by a benchmark, a model, a sample size with an optional seed (so different models receive the same questions), sampling parameters, a prompting protocol (system instruction, chain-ofthought cue or reproducibly drawn k-shot examples) and, optionally, tools.
Vision benchmarks can be run with images removed, as a text-only ablation on identical items.
Questions are answered by a single completion or inside an agent loop that uses the provider's native function calling or, failing that, a text protocol.

Tools (a Python interpreter, a calculator, file reading and eight bioinformatics sequence utilities) run in a sandbox: a separate Python process with CPU-time, memory and file-size limits, no network access and a fresh working directory per question (appendix p 5-6).
Every assistant turn, tool call and tool output is stored as an inspectable trajectory.
Answers are graded by deterministic rules; no LLM is used as a judge.

Multiple-choice answers are extracted by an ordered set of rules that recognises explicit answer statements and conclusion lines before falling back to isolated option letters, and the procedurally generated benchmarks store a typed answer (a number, sequence, list or label) that is compared exactly or, for decimal values, within a stated tolerance.
Reasoning traces are removed before grading; a reply truncated without an answer is retried once, and remaining empty replies are graded on the end of the reasoning trace, with both events flagged.

For each question the platform stores the prompt, raw reply, reasoning trace, extracted answer, correctness, tokens and latency, so grading rules can be improved and all runs re-scored without new inference (appendix pp 3-5).

To evaluate computational biology tasks rather than recall, the platform includes two procedurally generated benchmarks: BioCompute-Bench (300 single-step computations in 15 families, eg, translation, open reading frames, variant effect, CIGAR span, alignment score) and BioAgent-Bench (80 multi-step analyses over generated FASTA, VCF, GFF3, FASTQ and expression files, eg, splicing and translating a multi-exon gene).

Each item comes from its own seeded generator, so every installation produces identical items that do not exist on the web; ground truth is computed by the code that implements the sequence-analysis tools, and we recomputed all 380 answers independently with Biopython (appendix p 8).

We evaluated 12 open-weight models served by Ollama (version 0.32.14) on a shared institutional multi-GPU server: seven instruction models (Llama 3.1 8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen2.5 7B, Phi-4 14B, Gemma 3 12B, Gemma 3 27B and Llama 3.3 70B), four models that produce a reasoning trace before answering (DeepSeek-R1 7B, GLM-4.7-Flash, Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8 27B) and one additional vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL 7B).
Together they cover the main open model families, sizes from 7 to 70 billion parameters, instruction and reasoning models, and models with published scores on the benchmarks used.
Each build is identified by its Ollama digest.
All were 4-bit quantised builds (Q4_K_M) except Llama 3.1 8B (16-bit).
The context window was 32 768 tokens, temperature 0 unless stated, and the reply limit 2048 tokens for instruction models and 8192 for reasoning models and agent runs (appendix p 1).
All experiments were defined in a declarative plan and submitted as ordinary runs through the REST API by a client script, so every result is visible and auditable in the web interface.
Questions were sampled with seed 2026, so every model answered the same items.

The experiments addressed three questions: how locally measured accuracy compares with published scores (experiment 1); how much it varies with evaluation choices, namely answer extraction, prompting protocol and sampling temperature (answer-extraction analysis and experiments 2 and 3); and what models gain from images and tools, assessed by removing them (experiments 4 and 5).

In BioCompute-Bench, which assesses single-step computational tasks, each model answered the same 75 questions under two conditions: without access to tools (closed-book) and with access to the sandboxed Python interpreter and bioinformatics sequence utilities.

Accuracy is reported with Wilson 95% CIs.
Pooled medical accuracy is question-weighted across the biomedical benchmarks.

Because conditions were compared on identical items, paired differences between models, extraction rules, protocols, image conditions and tool conditions were tested with exact McNemar tests and reported with Newcombe hybrid score 95% CIs, with Holm correction within each experiment.

In experiment 1, a published score was considered compatible with our measurement if it lay within the measured 95% CI; because the CIs of these comparisons had half-widths of 5•7-13•4 points (150 questions per benchmark, 50 per MMLU subset), compatibility does not establish equivalence, and results for individual MMLU subsets are descriptive.

The number of questions needed to detect a paired protocol effect was estimated with the sample-size formula for McNemar's test, using the proportion of discordant questions observed in experiment 2 (appendix p 15).
In a sensitivity analysis, answers recovered from reasoning traces or obtained after truncation retries were excluded or counted as incorrect.
Analyses used Python (pandas, SciPy) in notebooks that read the platform's exports.

text.text: Compared with the final BenchmarkHub extraction rules, selecting the first standalone option letter reduced pooled medical accuracy by up to 14•0 percentage points, for Gemma 4 31B.
Selecting the last standalone option letter produced even larger accuracy reductions, reaching 33•1 percentage points for Gemma 3 27B.
Compared with the final rules on the same replies, these reductions were statistically significant after Holm correction for five and nine of the 11 models, respectively.

Both extraction methods also changed the relative ranking of models: with the first-letter rule, Qwen3.8 27B ranked first, whereas with the last-letter rule, Llama 3.3 70B ranked first and Gemma 3 27B fell to tenth place (appendix p 10).
The OpenAI simple-evals pattern, which searches for an explicit "Answer: X" statement, identified only 1-48% of replies as answerable, depending on the model.

Even the earlier and final versions of BenchmarkHub's own rules graded 997 of the 20 300 stored replies (4•9%) differently, changing pooled accuracy by up to 4•3 percentage points (Gemma 4 31B) and the rank of six models (appendix p0 10-11).
In experiment 2, changing the prompting protocol altered MedQA accuracy by -11•3 to +9•3 percentage points relative to the default prompt (figure 4B; appendix p 14-15).

text.text: The direction and magnitude of these changes depended on the model.
A chain-of-thought cue increased accuracy for Llama 3.1 8B by 9•3 percentage points (95% CI 1•0-17•5), but decreased accuracy for Qwen2.5 7B by 11•3 percentage points (4•0-18•4).
However, none of the 12 protocol comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm correction; the smallest adjusted p value was 0•055.
Approximately 19% of questions changed from correct to incorrect, or vice versa, between protocols.
Based on this observed discordance, approximately 600 questions would be required to detect a 5-percentage-point protocol effect with 80% power.
In experiment 3, repeated runs at temperature 0 produced identical results for both models.
At temperature 0•7, however, run-to-run variability differed between models.
Llama 3.1 8B achieved accuracies ranging from 51•3% to 59•3% across the three runs (SD 4•1 percentage points), with identical outcomes across all three runs for only 59•3% of questions.
Gemma 3 27B was substantially more stable, with accuracy ranging from 74•7% to 75•3% and identical outcomes across all three runs for 98•7% of questions (figure 4C; appendix p 15).

BenchmarkHub makes model evaluation a recorded, repeatable and locally executable procedure.

Using it on 12 open-weight models, we found that the answer-extraction rule alone changed medical accuracy by more than the differences between many models and reordered the leaderboard, that published scores were usually higher than those measured under a documented protocol, and that image availability and tool access changed results substantially, whereas prompting-protocol effects of up to 11 points could not be estimated precisely with 150 questions.
A single number on a model card therefore says little unless the procedure that produced it is reported and can be rerun.
Answer extraction is usually treated as an implementation detail, but it was the largest source of variation among the evaluation settings we examined.

Sensitivity to prompt format and answer extraction has been documented on general tasks, [14] [15] [16] and harness developers name extraction and normalisation as recurrent sources of irreproducibility; 18 we show that on medical benchmarks simple rules found in evaluation scripts change accuracy by up to 33 points for the same replies, penalising models for their reply style rather than their knowledge, and that even careful revisions of a rule move scores and ranks.

text.text: Because the platform keeps every raw reply, extraction rules can be compared and audited after the fact, and all runs rescored without new inference.
Medical evaluations should report their extraction rules and, ideally, release raw replies.

The gap with published scores, largest on MMLU-Pro, is consistent with those scores having been obtained with different prompting protocols and internal frameworks; quantisation is an unlikely sole explanation, because the largest gap was for the only model served with 16-bit weights.
It illustrates why published and locally measured numbers should not be compared without their protocols.

Typical medical evaluation sizes are also too small to estimate protocol effects: with 150 questions, differences of about 10 points between prompts were compatible with chance, and several hundred questions per condition are needed.

Temperature 0 gave identical repeats in our setting, in which one local server processed requests without batching, but it does not guarantee reproducibility in general: when models are run through APIs or with batched inference, outputs at temperature 0 still vary between runs, 17, 28 so serving conditions belong in the methods of any evaluation and repeated runs are advisable.

text.text: The image ablation shows that multimodal accuracy can overstate visual understanding.

Textonly shortcuts have been documented for general multimodal benchmarks 19 and flawed visual reasoning behind correct answers for medical image challenges. 20 MedXpertQA MM was filtered for difficulty rather than for image necessity, 24 and its original report did not include a text-only baseline; the two strongest models answered half of its items correctly without the image, and no model gained significantly from it.

text.text: On MMMU 26 medical subjects, by contrast, the strongest models clearly used the image.
Running every vision benchmark with and without images is a cheap control that the platform performs on identical items.
The agentic experiment adds a dimension that static question answering misses.

Biology benchmarks without tools show that LLMs handle sequence manipulation poorly, 29 and agentic benchmarks over real analyses remain far from solved. 30 On our procedurally generated tasks, a sandboxed interpreter converted near-zero closed-book accuracy on character-level computations into near-perfect accuracy for the larger models, and multi-step analyses depended on writing code rather than on the predefined sequence tools, whereas small models stopped early or looped through failing tool calls.

text.text: Procedural generation with computed, independently verified ground truth makes these benchmarks exactly gradable and resistant to memorisation, and the stored trajectories make agent failures diagnosable.
For health systems, running open-weight models on premises is attractive for data protection but shifts the burden of evaluation to the institution.

BenchmarkHub lets a hospital or research group evaluate models on public benchmarks and its own questions without data leaving its infrastructure, compare them under identical documented conditions with paired statistics, and export complete records for audit, as recommended by reporting guidance for LLM studies. 27 Such evaluations are a screening step: benchmark accuracy is not clinical utility, [7] [8] [9] and our results add that even benchmark accuracy is conditional on the evaluation procedure.

text.text: Benchmarks were sampled (150 questions per benchmark, 50 per MMLU subset), so individual accuracies carry CIs of about ±6-8 points (±10-14 for MMLU subsets) and protocol effects were underpowered; the platform can run complete benchmarks.
The final extraction rules were refined on replies from the same models and may be less accurate for other models.
All but one model were 4-bit builds, which may explain part of the differences from published scores, and the published scores available were few and heterogeneous in protocol.
The generated benchmarks cover well defined computational tasks rather than open research questions.
The sandbox limits resources and blocks network access but does not isolate the filesystem or filter system calls, so untrusted models require a container or virtual machine (appendix p 6).
Finally, all benchmarks were in English and none used real patient records.
In conclusion, medical benchmark results depend on how they are produced.
Open, selfhosted evaluation infrastructure that records each step allows institutions to reproduce, audit and extend claims about LLMs before considering them for clinical use.

text.text: The largest improvements were observed in task families requiring character-level sequence manipulation, such as reverse-complement generation and translation, which models rarely solved without tools but usually solved when the relevant tools were available (figure6B).
Performance on the multi-step BioAgent-Bench tasks varied markedly between models (figure6C).
Gemma 4 31B solved all 40 tasks (100•0%), and Qwen3.8 27B solved 39 (97•5%).
In contrast, Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen2.5 7B each solved one task (2•5%), while Llama 3.3 70B solved two (5•0%).
Tool-trajectory analysis showed that successful multi-step analyses generally required the Python interpreter: 83 of the 86 correctly solved model-task instances involved Python.
By comparison, only one of the 25 tasks attempted using sequence tools alone was solved.

For single-step BioCompute-Bench tasks, sequence tools alone were used successfully in a similar proportion of the tasks in which they were invoked as Python (83% versus 80%, respectively; appendix pp16-17).
The recorded trajectories also revealed different failure patterns.
Llama 3.3 70B typically stopped after a single tool call, whereas Qwen2.5 7B made a mean of 48 tool calls per task, most of them to sequence utilities, with frequent errors.
Finally, independent recomputation reproduced the stored ground-truth answers for all 380 procedurally generated benchmark items (appendix p 8).
